newsitem.title: USA: Group to market privacy system for Net surfers.
newsitem.headline: Group to market privacy system for Net surfers.

text.p: The Electronic Frontier Foundation and CommerceNet said Wednesday they would launch a service early next year to protect the privacy of Internet surfers.

Aiming to ease consumer concerns about Web sites collecting their names and other vital information and marketing it, the two groups set up a system to discourage commercial firms from tracking someone's online travels.

It involves a voluntary accreditation system for businesses with commercial Web sites, in which accredited companies would disclose on their Web site how much of a visitor's information is being collected.
Currently, people surfing the Net with even casual visits to different Web sites are leaving an electronic trail of their visits, often including lots of detail beyond their name.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a group concerned with civil liberties in the online world, has been working on the privacy system, dubbed eTRUST, for months. It unveiled the plan to make the system commercial in early 1997 at a meeting held by CommerceNet in Burlingame, a city just south of San Francisco. CommerceNet is a non-profit group organised to promote electronic commerce.
Several companies are involved in the eTRUST effort, including accountants Coopers & Lybrand and KPMG Peat Marwick, and Portland Software, which is helping to develop the system.
